summary: Clark County, AR steel lookout of the Arkansas Forestry Commission; 1941 survey says about 100 ft, 1957 note says 110 ft and good condition; no later record found.

facts.design: Steel tower with an enclosed cab at the top (1941 description); the 1957 recovery note describes a glass-enclosed observation cab on a four-legged steel structure
facts.status_note: The last recorded condition is a 1957 survey note listing the station as good; no later source confirms whether the tower stands

events.note: Coast and Geodetic Survey description: lookout tower of the Arkansas Forestry Commission, steel, about 100 feet, enclosed cab; the station was not visited
Recovery note: glass-enclosed observation cab on a four-legged steel structure, overall height 110 feet; condition listed as good; probably the same station as in 1941

evidence.supports: site is in Clark County, about 4.5 miles NE of Whelen Springs
1941 description calls it a lookout tower of the Arkansas Forestry Commission

evidence.supports: Preserve Arkansas says the state's lookout towers were built to guard against wildfire

evidence.supports: Arkansas has fourteen lookouts on the National Historic Lookout Register; Bull Mountain is not among the named sites
evidence.quote: Arkansas has fourteen lookouts on the National Historic Lookout Register

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1941 description gives about 100 feet (30.5 m); the 1957 recovery note gives an overall height of 110 feet (about 33.5 m). The record keeps 30.5 m from the first description; the sources do not explain the difference.

sources.title: Bull Mountain Fire Lot (PID DL1426), datasheet

notes_for_editor: The NGS datasheet (1941 and 1957 entries) is the only primary source. Not found: construction date, staffing, fires, fate after 1957, access. Access and visit facts are not set. The brief's coordinates match the NGS position (33.8737, -93.0629). Search snippets mentioned a 110-foot steel former tower near Alpine in Clark County; unverified and not used, though the 110-foot height is similar and it may be worth checking. Preserve Arkansas's 1920s-1930s date range and its CCC attribution are not used in the story.
